description.en: The back lever is an advanced gymnastics hold where you hang from a bar or rings and extend your body horizontally below the bar, face up. It requires elite straight-arm strength through the shoulders, lats, and core. It is a foundational skill in gymnastics strength training.

en: Hang from a bar or rings. Pull yourself up and over into a skin-the-cat position (inverted hang).
Slowly lower your body from the inverted position toward horizontal.
Extend your body until it is parallel to the ground, face up, below the bar.
Hold the horizontal position. Arms are straight above you gripping the bar.
Start with a tucked back lever (knees to chest) and progress to full.
Progressions: tuck → advanced tuck → straddle → full.
Hold for 5 to 15 seconds at each progression level.
This is an advanced skill requiring months of progression.
Builds elite straight-arm strength
Foundational gymnastics skill
Develops shoulder, lat, and core strength
Impressive calisthenics achievement
Builds body control and awareness
Progressive skill with clear progressions

description.en: The band close-grip row is a band rowing variation with hands positioned close together for increased bicep involvement and lower lat emphasis. It can be performed seated or standing, mimicking a close-grip cable row.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height in front of you, or sit on the floor with band looped around your feet.
Grip both ends of the band with hands close together (6 to 12 inches apart), palms facing each other.
Start with arms extended forward.
Row the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back along your sides.
Squeeze your lats and biceps at the end of the row.
Slowly extend forward under control.
Keep your torso upright.
Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Close grip increases bicep involvement
Emphasizes the lower lats
Mimics close-grip cable row
Highly portable
Easy to scale
Builds back thickness

description.en: The band concentration curl is a single-arm bicep isolation exercise performed seated with a resistance band looped under one foot. Your elbow braces against your inner thigh, eliminating body english and isolating the bicep. It is the at-home version of the dumbbell concentration curl.

en: Sit on a chair or bench. Loop a resistance band under your right foot.
Hold the other end of the band with your right hand.
Place the back of your right upper arm (just above the elbow) against your right inner thigh.
Start with your arm extended and the band taut.
Curl your right hand toward your right shoulder by bending at the elbow.
Squeeze your bicep hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds.
Lower under control over two seconds.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Strict bicep isolation — no body english
Builds the bicep peak
Highly portable
Easy to scale by band thickness
Useful when no dumbbells are available
Joint-friendly

description.en: The barbell bench press with 2 boards places 2 wooden boards on the chest, raising the bottom position of the press. The shorter range of motion lets you handle more weight than a full bench press, building lockout strength and triceps power. More boards means a shorter range and heavier loading.

en: Have a training partner hold 2 boards on your chest, or strap them onto your shirt.
Lie on a flat bench under the loaded barbell.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar with control until it touches the top board.
Press the bar back up explosively, locking out at the top.
Re-rack the bar carefully when finished.
Partial range allows heavier loads than full bench
Builds lockout and triceps strength
Different board heights target different sticking points
Reduces stress on the shoulders
Common method in powerlifting accessory work
Helps overcome bench press plateaus

description.en: The barbell bent over wide alternate row plus is a strong upper back builder. The lifter grips a barbell wide and bends over with a flat back, then alternates pulling each side of the bar up to the body. The wide grip targets the upper back and lats hard.

en: Set up a barbell on the floor or low rack.
Grip the bar with a wide overhand grip outside shoulder width.
Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back.
Brace your core and let the bar hang at arms length.
Pull one side of the bar up toward the lower chest.
Squeeze the upper back hard at the top.
Lower that side back down as you pull the other side up.
Continue alternating row pulls.
Strong upper back builder
Trains the lats wide grip
Builds back thickness
Strong unilateral focus
Useful back move
Builds rotational core

description.en: The barbell decline wide grip pullover is performed on a decline bench with a wide grip on the barbell. The wider grip changes the lat angle and emphasizes back width. The decline position increases the stretch on the lats and chest. It is excellent for back and chest hypertrophy.

en: Lie on a decline bench with feet hooked under the pads.
Hold a barbell over your chest with a grip wider than shoulder-width.
Use a pronated grip with palms facing forward.
Brace your core and keep your back against the bench.
Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
Lower the bar back behind your head in an arc.
Continue until you feel a deep lat and chest stretch.
Pull the bar back over your chest using the lats.
Deep lat stretch
Builds back width
Decline angle increases stretch
Strong upper torso builder
Builds the chest and lats
Wide grip biases the back

description.en: The barbell full clean (squat clean) is the full Olympic lift where you pull the bar from the floor and catch it in a full front squat position. It is more demanding than the power clean because you must squat the bar up after the catch, requiring full mobility and technical precision.

en: Stand over the barbell with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Drop your hips low. Chest up. Shoulders over the bar.
Pull the bar from the floor by extending your legs — keep the bar close to your body.
As the bar passes your knees, explosively extend your hips and shrug.
Pull yourself under the bar and catch it in a full front squat — bar across your front shoulders, hips below parallel.
Stand up from the front squat to complete the lift.
Lower the bar back to the floor with control.
Master the power clean before attempting full cleans.
Full Olympic clean — competition lift
Builds total-body explosive power
Develops front squat strength
Tests mobility and coordination
Trains catching at maximum depth
Allows heavier loads than power clean

description.en: The barbell incline wide reverse grip bench press combines three chest-focused techniques. The incline angle hits the upper pec, the wide grip emphasizes the outer chest, and the reverse (underhand) grip reduces front delt involvement. The combination targets the upper chest with reduced shoulder strain.

en: Set a bench to a 30 to 45 degree incline.
Lie back with eyes under the bar.
Grip the bar with palms facing you (underhand grip), wider than shoulder-width.
Pull your shoulder blades back and engage your lats.
Use a spotter to safely hand off the bar.
Hold the bar over your upper chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar with control to your upper chest.
Press the bar back up by squeezing the upper chest. Lock out at the top.
Targets upper chest fibers heavily
Wide grip emphasizes outer pec
Reverse grip reduces shoulder strain
Triple-emphasis on chest development
Useful upper chest specialization variation
Builds chest detail in the clavicular head

description.en: The barbell preacher curl is a bicep curl performed with the upper arms braced against an angled preacher bench pad while curling a barbell. The fixed arm position eliminates body english and isolates the biceps brachii completely. It is one of the most effective and time-tested exercises for building bicep size with strict form.

en: Adjust the preacher bench so the top of the pad sits comfortably under your armpits when seated.
Sit on the bench with your chest against the pad and both upper arms draped fully along the angled side.
Have a partner hand you the barbell, or pick it up before sitting down. Use an underhand (supinated) grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Start with the barbell at the top position and arms fully extended downward along the pad. Brace your core.
Lower the barbell under control over two to three seconds until your arms are nearly fully extended. Stop just before your elbows lock out.
Curl the barbell back up by bending only at the elbows. Keep your upper arms pressed firmly against the pad.
Continue until your forearms are roughly vertical. Squeeze your biceps hard at the top.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use an EZ bar instead if a straight barbell bothers your wrists.
Isolates the biceps brachii almost entirely
Eliminates body english — strict form is forced by the bench
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell preacher curls
Builds bicep strength at the bottom (lengthened) position
Excellent for high-rep bicep finishing work
Trains both arms simultaneously for equal effort

description.en: The barbell rear lunge II is a variation of the standard barbell reverse lunge, typically performed with a deeper step or a slightly different stance to emphasize specific muscle groups. The barbell loading allows progressive overload while the reverse lunge pattern reduces knee stress compared to forward lunges.

en: Position a barbell across your upper back as in a back squat.
Stand with feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core and lift your chest.
Step back with your right leg into a deep reverse lunge.
Lower until your back knee approaches the floor.
Keep most of your weight on the front leg.
Drive through the front foot to step back to the starting position.
Repeat on the other leg, alternating sides.
Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally
Reverse lunge pattern is knee-friendly
Barbell allows heavy loading
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong core engagement
Useful accessory for squatters

description.en: The barbell standing front raise over head is an extended front raise that continues lifting the bar past shoulder height up overhead. The full range of motion trains the front delts through their full action and adds upper trap involvement at the overhead position. It is a strong choice for shoulder and trap training.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a barbell with both hands.
Position your hands shoulder-width apart with palms facing down.
Hold the bar at thigh level with arms extended.
Maintain a slight bend in the elbows.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Raise the bar in front of you in an arc.
Continue past shoulder height up to fully overhead.
Lower the bar back down with control to the starting position.
Extended range of motion
Builds front delts through full range
Adds upper trap involvement
Different stimulus than standard front raise
Useful for shoulder and trap training
Strong overhead lockout work

description.en: The bench dip on stability ball is a tricep dip variation with the feet on a stability ball. The unstable feet position challenges the core and adds difficulty to the dip. It builds the triceps and core stability.

en: Sit on the edge of a bench with hands gripping the edge.
Place the feet on top of a stability ball.
Slide the hips off the bench.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lower the hips down by bending the elbows.
Stop when the elbows reach about ninety degrees.
Press through the palms to lock the elbows.
Continue for the working set.
Trains the triceps
Builds core stability
Strong dip variation
Useful unstable surface
Builds the upper arms

description.en: The bench dip with legs on bench is a harder bench dip variation. Setting the feet on a second bench elevates the body and forces the triceps to support more bodyweight than a standard bench dip.

en: Place two benches parallel about leg length apart.
Sit on one bench and grip the edge with hands shoulder width apart.
Place your heels on the second bench with legs straight.
Lift the hips off the bench so your arms support your weight.
Bend the elbows and lower your hips toward the floor.
Keep the elbows tracking back and not flaring out.
Stop when the upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Press through the palms back up to lockout and repeat.
Hits the triceps hard with elevated bodyweight loading.
Engages the chest and front deltoids as supporting movers.
Builds upper body pushing strength without weights.
Easy to scale by adjusting bench heights.
Develops shoulder stability under bodyweight load.
Travel friendly with minimal equipment.

description.en: The bent leg kicks is a quadruped glute kickback performed on all fours. The lifter keeps the working leg bent at 90 degrees and kicks the heel up toward the ceiling. The bent leg position keeps tension on the glutes through full hip extension.

en: Get on your hands and knees in a tabletop position.
Set the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips.
Keep the working leg bent at 90 degrees.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Kick the bent leg up driving the heel toward the ceiling.
Squeeze the glute hard at the top.
Lower the knee back down with control.
Complete reps and switch legs.
Strong glute isolator
No equipment needed
Easy to scale
Builds glute size
Trains hip extension
Useful glute finisher

description.en: The bodyweight drop jump squat performs a fast drop into a squat position followed by an explosive jump up. The reactive nature of the drop trains the stretch-shortening cycle and builds powerful lower body explosiveness. It is a strong choice for athletic plyometric training.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Drop down quickly into a squat position by bending the knees and hips.
Land softly with knees tracking over the toes.
Continue down until thighs are parallel to the floor.
As soon as you reach the bottom, drive up explosively.
Jump up off the floor with full extension.
Land softly and reset for the next rep.
Builds reactive lower body power
Trains the stretch-shortening cycle
Strong plyometric stimulus
No equipment required
Develops athletic explosiveness
Useful for sports training

description.en: The bottle weighted bent over reverse fly is a no equipment shoulder drill using filled water bottles as light dumbbells. Hinging forward and lifting the arms out to the sides loads the rear delts and upper back.

en: Hold a filled water bottle in each hand.
Hinge forward at the hips with the back flat.
Set the arms hanging straight down with a slight elbow bend.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Pull the hands out to the sides in a fly motion.
Squeeze the rear delts hard at the top.
Return with control to the start.
Continue for the working set.
Trains the rear delts at home.
No gym equipment required.
Builds the upper back.
Useful for travel.
Improves posture.

description.en: The bottle weighted lying chest press uses weighted water bottles for an at-home floor press. The lifter lies on the floor or a bench and presses the bottles up over the chest. The floor stops the bottoming out and protects the shoulders.

en: Lie on your back on the floor or a bench.
Hold a weighted bottle in each hand at chest height.
Bend the elbows so the upper arms rest on the floor.
Brace your core and squeeze the chest.
Press the bottles straight up to lockout above the chest.
Squeeze the chest hard at the top.
Lower the bottles back down with control until the elbows touch the floor.
Press back up to lockout for the next rep.
Strong at-home chest builder
No dumbbells required
Builds the chest
Travel-friendly setup
Useful chest builder
Floor protects the shoulders

description.en: The cable close-grip curl performs standing cable curls with hands positioned closer than shoulder-width on the bar. The narrow grip shifts emphasis to the long (outer) head of the biceps, building bicep width when viewed from the front.

en: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar or EZ bar.
Grip the bar with hands about 6 inches apart (narrow grip), palms up.
Stand tall. Pin your elbows at your sides.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Squeeze your biceps at the top. Focus on the outer head contraction.
Lower under control over two seconds.
Keep your upper arms still — only your forearms move.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Emphasizes the long (outer) head of the bicep
Builds bicep width from the front
Constant cable tension
Easy to load progressively
Different stimulus than wide-grip curls
Useful for complete bicep development

description.en: The cable kneeling triceps extension is a tricep isolation exercise where you kneel facing away from a high cable pulley with a rope attachment and extend at the elbows to push the rope forward. The kneeling position eliminates leg drive and lower-back involvement, isolating the triceps strictly.

en: Attach a rope to a high cable pulley. Kneel facing away from the cable machine.
Grip both ends of the rope. Pull them behind your head with elbows bent.
Pin your upper arms next to your head. Elbows point forward.
Brace your core. Keep your torso upright.
Extend at the elbows to push the rope forward and up. Split the rope at lockout.
Squeeze your triceps hard. Hold one second.
Slowly let the rope return behind your head over two seconds.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Kneeling position eliminates leg drive and lower-back involvement
Constant cable tension throughout
Strict tricep isolation
Deep stretch on the long head
Easy to load progressively
Useful variation for high-rep tricep work

description.en: The cable lying close grip curl is performed lying on your back on the floor with a low cable above your head. Using a close grip on the cable attachment, you curl through a strict bicep range. The lying position eliminates body english entirely and the close grip emphasizes the long head of the biceps.

en: Set a cable to the lowest pulley with a short bar attachment.
Lie on your back on the floor with feet near the cable station.
Grip the bar with a close underhand grip.
Extend your arms straight up over your chest with the cable creating tension.
Brace your core and press your back to the floor.
Lower the bar back toward your forehead by bending only at the elbows.
Continue down until the bar is near your forehead.
Curl back up to the starting position by extending the elbows.
Strict bicep isolation
Lying position eliminates body english
Constant cable tension through the range
Close grip targets long head
Useful for breaking through curl plateaus
Strong peak contraction

description.en: The cable shoulder press uses two low cable pulleys to perform an overhead press with constant cable tension. You face away from the cables, hold D-handles at your shoulders, and press overhead. The cables provide resistance throughout — including at lockout where free weights lose tension.

en: Set two cable pulleys to the lowest position. Attach D-handles.
Face away from the cables. Grip both handles at shoulder height.
Stand in a staggered stance for stability.
Press both handles overhead to lockout.
Squeeze your shoulders and triceps at the top. Constant cable tension here.
Lower back to your shoulders under control.
Brace your core throughout.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Constant cable tension through full press
Tension at lockout unlike free weights
Easy to load progressively
Standing position adds core demand
Joint-friendly
Excellent for shoulder hypertrophy

description.en: The cable standing one leg calf raise is performed standing on one foot with a cable attached to a belt or held in the same-side hand. The single-leg setup doubles the load on the working calf and adds balance demands. It is a great accessory for calf hypertrophy.

en: Attach a low cable to a belt at your waist or hold a handle in one hand.
Stand on one foot facing away from the cable.
Position the working foot on a small block with the heel hanging off.
Lift the other foot off the floor.
Hold a wall or rack for balance.
Brace your core and keep the standing leg slightly bent.
Press up onto your toes by lifting your heel high.
Lower slowly to a deep stretch. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Targets the calves unilaterally
Constant cable tension
Trains balance
Strong calf builder
Reduces strength imbalances
Builds calf size

description.en: The dumbbell floor fly is a chest isolation exercise performed lying flat on the floor instead of on a bench. The floor stops the dumbbells from descending below your torso, limiting the bottom range and providing a built-in safety stop. It is an excellent variation for lifters with shoulder issues, beginners learning the fly pattern, or anyone training at home without a bench.

en: Lie flat on the floor with a dumbbell in each hand. Bend your knees with feet flat on the floor.
Press the dumbbells straight up over your chest with arms fully extended and palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Brace your core and pull your shoulders down and back into the floor.
Set a slight bend in your elbows and lock that angle in throughout the lift.
Lower the dumbbells out to your sides in a wide arc until your upper arms touch the floor.
Pause briefly with the dumbbells touching the floor — this is the safety stop the bench would not provide.
Reverse the arc by squeezing your chest to bring the dumbbells back up over your chest.
Squeeze your chest hard at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Limited bottom range protects the shoulders from overextension
Built-in safety stop — the floor catches the dumbbells
Excellent for lifters with shoulder issues
Works at home without a bench
Easier than bench flies for beginners learning the pattern
Builds the chest with reduced shoulder strain

description.en: The dumbbell good morning squat is a combo lift that pairs a good morning hinge with a full squat. The good morning loads the hamstrings and lower back, then the squat hits the quads and glutes. It builds total leg strength and trains hip and knee dominant patterns together.

en: Stand tall with a dumbbell held in each hand on your shoulders.
Keep feet shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core and keep your back flat.
Hinge at the hips and lower your torso forward like a good morning.
Stop when your torso is roughly parallel to the floor.
Return to standing by extending the hips.
From standing, squat down by sitting your hips back and bending the knees.
Drive up to standing. Each rep is one good morning plus one squat.
Trains hinge and squat together
Builds the full posterior chain
Hits the quads and glutes
Time-efficient combo movement
Improves hip and knee mobility
Useful for athletic conditioning

description.en: The dumbbell reverse grip biceps curl is performed with an overhand (pronated) grip on the dumbbells rather than the standard underhand grip. The pronated grip shifts emphasis from the biceps to the brachioradialis and forearm extensors, building forearm size and grip while still working the biceps.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at thigh level with palms facing back.
Pin your elbows against your sides.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Curl both dumbbells up by bending at the elbows while maintaining the overhand grip.
Continue until the dumbbells are near shoulder height.
Squeeze the forearms and biceps at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back down with control to full extension.
Targets brachioradialis and forearm extensors
Builds forearm size and grip
Different stimulus than standard curls
Useful for thicker arms
Pairs well with regular curls
Strong wrist stability work

description.en: The dumbbell single power clean is a single-arm version of the Olympic power clean using a dumbbell instead of a barbell. The lift brings the dumbbell from the floor to the shoulder in one explosive motion. The single-arm pattern adds rotational and lateral stability demand on top of the standard explosive power work.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, a dumbbell on the floor between your feet.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the dumbbell with one hand.
Keep the other arm extended out for balance.
Pull your shoulders back and engage your lats.
Brace your core hard.
Drive through your heels to start the dumbbell moving up.
As the dumbbell passes your hips, drop into a partial squat while pulling the dumbbell to your shoulder.
Stand up to the lockout position with the dumbbell at your shoulder. Lower with control. Switch arms.
Builds explosive total body power
Strong unilateral loading pattern
Develops Olympic lifting skill
Functional carryover to athletic movement
Time-efficient compound lift
Trains hip drive and shoulder catch

description.en: The elbow to knee side plank crunch is a side plank variation that adds a crunching motion. The lifter holds a side plank and brings the top elbow to the top knee. It is a strong oblique builder.

en: Lie on the side with the bottom forearm on the floor.
Stack the feet and legs straight.
Brace your core and lift the hips into a side plank.
Place the top hand behind the head with the elbow flared.
Lift the top knee up toward the top elbow.
Crunch the elbow down to meet the knee.
Pause briefly at the contracted position.
Extend back to start. Finish then switch sides.
Loads the obliques
Strong side plank variation
Builds the core
Useful for core size
Trains the side abs

description.en: The elbows back stretch is a chest opener performed by clasping your hands behind your head with elbows wide, then pulling your elbows backward to open the chest and front shoulders. It is similar to the behind-head chest stretch but emphasizes pulling the elbows further back to deepen the stretch.

en: Stand or sit tall with shoulders pulled back and down.
Clasp your hands behind your head with elbows wide.
Pull your elbows back, opening your chest as much as possible.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Lift your chest tall. Avoid arching your lower back.
Feel the deep stretch across your chest and front shoulders.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Release and repeat 2 to 3 times.
Deeply opens the chest and front shoulders
Counteracts forward-rounded posture
Quick and accessible
No equipment needed
Excellent post-workout stretch
Improves overhead pressing position

description.en: The exercise ball one-legged diagonal kick hamstring curl is an advanced stability ball hamstring exercise. You lie on your back with both feet on the ball, lift one leg up diagonally, and curl the ball toward you with the other leg. The single-leg curl combined with the diagonal kick creates extreme instability and hamstring challenge.

en: Lie on your back with both heels on top of a stability ball. Arms at your sides, palms down.
Lift your hips up into a bridge position. Body forms a line from heels to shoulders.
Lift your left leg straight up off the ball, extending it diagonally to about 45 degrees.
Curl the ball toward you with your right heel by bending your right knee.
Continue curling until the ball is under your right foot.
Slowly extend your right leg to push the ball back out.
Maintain the bridge and the left leg lift throughout.
Complete reps on one side, then switch legs. Use slow, controlled movement.
Extreme hamstring and glute challenge
Single-leg work exposes imbalances
Heavy core and hip stability demand
Builds functional hamstring strength
Engages deep stabilizers
Advanced stability ball progression

description.en: The front plank with arm lift is a plank variation where you hold a high plank position and alternately lift one arm off the floor at a time, reaching forward. The single-arm lift creates significant anti-rotation core demand and engages the shoulders alongside the core.

en: Get into a high plank position on your hands and toes. Hands directly under shoulders. Body straight from heels to head.
Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes.
Slowly lift your right hand off the floor and reach it forward at shoulder height.
Keep your hips perfectly level. Do not let them rotate or tilt.
Hold for one to two seconds.
Lower your right hand back to the floor under control.
Lift your left hand with the same form. Continue alternating.
Perform 6 to 10 lifts per arm per set. Move with control.
Adds significant anti-rotation core demand
Engages the shoulders and serratus anterior
Trains hip and core stability
More challenging than a static plank
No equipment needed
Excellent core finisher

description.en: The full squat mobility hold (deep squat hold or Asian squat) sits in the deepest possible squat position and holds it for time. It develops hip, ankle, and thoracic mobility simultaneously. It is essentially the same exercise as the potty squat under a different name.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out.
Squat down as deep as possible — hips below knees.
Keep heels on the floor. Widen stance or angle toes more if heels rise.
Hold the deep position. Arms forward for counterbalance.
Breathe deeply and relax into the position.
Hold for 30 to 120 seconds.
Use a support (pole, rack) if you cannot hold unsupported.
Practice daily for best mobility gains.
Develops deep squat mobility
Improves hip, ankle, and thoracic flexibility
Foundational human movement pattern
No equipment needed
Daily practice yields best results
Reveals and addresses mobility limitations

description.en: The heel glute bridge is a glute bridge variation performed with the toes lifted off the floor and weight pushed through the heels only. The toes-up position increases hamstring activation while still loading the glutes heavily. It is an effective bodyweight posterior chain exercise.

en: Lie flat on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Lift your toes off the floor. Keep only your heels in contact with the ground.
Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor.
Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips off the floor.
Continue lifting until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Squeeze your glutes and hamstrings hard at the top for one to two seconds.
Lower under control back to the floor.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Increases hamstring activation vs standard glute bridge
Builds the glutes and hamstrings together
No equipment needed
Easy to scale by adding weight or single-leg variation
Useful warm-up before deadlifts
Reduces quad involvement vs standard bridge

description.en: The high jump rope is a jump-rope variation where you drive your knees high with each rope rotation, combining jump rope conditioning with high-knee running. It dramatically increases the hip-flexor demand and cardiovascular intensity compared to standard jumping.

en: Hold the jump rope handles. Start with feet together.
Begin jumping rope with alternating feet (skip style).
Drive each knee as high as possible with every rotation — aim for hip height or higher.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Pump your arms for balance.
Maintain rhythm with the rope while keeping the knee drive aggressive.
This is very demanding — start with short intervals (20 to 30 seconds).
Rest between intervals. Build up duration over time.
Focus on height of knee drive, not just speed.
Dramatically increases cardiovascular demand
Builds hip-flexor strength and endurance
Combines jump rope conditioning with high-knee running
Excellent HIIT interval exercise
Burns calories at a very high rate
Builds coordination under fatigue

description.en: The kettlebell bent press is an old-time strongman lift where you hold a KB in the front rack and press it overhead by bending your torso away from the KB rather than pressing the KB up. Your body bends down while the KB stays in place above — then you stand up to lockout. It requires excellent mobility and body control.

en: Clean a KB to the right front rack. Stand with feet wider than hip-width.
Turn your feet to the left (about 45 degrees).
Begin bending your torso to the left. At the same time, extend your right arm upward.
The KB stays roughly in place while your body lowers under it.
Continue bending until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor with the KB locked out overhead.
Look up at the KB throughout.
Stand back up with the KB overhead by reversing the lateral bend.
Use light weight until technique is solid. Aim for 3 to 5 reps per side.
Old-time strongman skill
Builds extraordinary lateral core and shoulder strength
Develops overhead mobility under lateral bend
Tests total-body control and flexibility
Allows pressing very heavy weight overhead
Impressive demonstration of strength

description.en: The kettlebell burpee is a brutal full-body conditioning exercise that combines a burpee with a kettlebell deadlift, jump back to push-up, return, and overhead press. It hits virtually every muscle group while delivering elite cardiovascular conditioning in a single movement.

en: Stand with a kettlebell on the floor between your feet. Hands on your hips.
Hinge down and grip the kettlebell with both hands.
From the hinge position, jump or step both feet back into a high plank position. Hands on the kettlebell handle.
Lower into a push-up if able. Press back up.
Jump or step your feet back to your hands.
Stand up while lifting the kettlebell to your chest.
Press the kettlebell overhead with both hands to lockout.
Lower the kettlebell back to the floor. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Brutal full-body conditioning in one movement
Trains the chest, legs, shoulders, and core simultaneously
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Builds work capacity
Time-efficient compound exercise
Burns calories at a very high rate

description.en: The leg raise dragon flag is an elite abs move popularized by Bruce Lee. The lifter lies on a bench and grips a support overhead, then lifts the entire body up keeping it straight. The body pivots on the upper back while the abs hold the body straight against gravity.

en: Lie on a flat bench.
Reach overhead and grip a sturdy support behind the head.
Pinch the shoulder blades and brace your core hard.
Lift the entire body up by driving the legs straight up.
Keep the body in a straight line from feet to shoulders.
At the top the body should be vertical with weight on upper back.
Lower the body back down slowly keeping it straight.
Stop just above the bench. Repeat without touching down.
Elite abs builder
Trains full body tension
Builds full ab strength
Useful for advanced trainees
Strong calisthenic move
Builds core size

description.en: The lying back extension with press is a combo move performed face down on the floor. The lifter extends the back to lift the chest off the floor and presses the arms overhead at the same time. The combination builds back, glutes, and shoulder strength together.

en: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended overhead.
Make loose fists with palms facing each other.
Brace your core and keep your head neutral.
Lift your chest off the floor by extending the back.
At the same time press your arms forward and overhead.
Reach high with the hands as the chest rises.
Pause briefly at the top and squeeze the back and glutes.
Lower the chest and arms back to the floor with control.
Trains back and shoulders together
Builds posterior chain
No equipment needed
Useful for posture
Combo move saves time
Easy to add to any session

description.en: The myotatic crunch on bosu ball is a full range crunch done over a bosu ball. The lifter lies back over the dome side of the bosu to extend the spine, then crunches up. The extra range of motion loads the abs harder than a flat crunch.

en: Sit on a bosu ball with feet flat on the floor.
Walk the feet out and lie back so the lower back is over the dome.
Allow the spine to extend backward over the ball.
Place the hands behind the head.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Curl the torso up and forward into a crunch.
Squeeze the abs hard at the top.
Lower with control back over the ball.
Full range crunch
Loads the abs through extra range
Strong ab builder
Useful for core size
Builds the rectus abdominis

description.en: The resistance band foot inversion is an ankle strength drill targeting the muscles that invert the foot. The lifter loops a band around the foot and pulls the foot inward against the band resistance. The move strengthens the tibialis posterior and inner ankle.

en: Sit on the floor with one leg straight in front.
Loop a resistance band around the working foot.
Anchor the other end to a stable point on the outside.
Brace your core and keep the leg still.
Rotate the foot inward against the band.
Squeeze the inside of the lower leg at the end range.
Return the foot to the start with control.
Complete reps and switch feet.
Strengthens the inner ankle
Builds ankle stability
Useful rehab move
No major equipment needed
Strong for runners
Easy to add to a warm-up

description.en: The resistance band skier mimics the cross-country ski machine using a resistance band anchored overhead. Holding both ends of the band, you pull down and back simultaneously like a ski pole motion. The continuous pulling pattern combines cardio with strong lat and tricep work.

en: Anchor a resistance band overhead to a pull up bar or anchor point.
Grip both ends of the band with arms extended overhead.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, soft bend in the knees.
Lean forward slightly at the hips.
Brace your core.
Pull both bands down and back along your sides simultaneously.
Continue until your hands reach hip level.
Slowly extend the arms back overhead and repeat at a steady pace.
Combines cardio with back and tricep work
Mimics cross-country ski motion
Strong lat engagement
Builds upper body endurance
Easy to scale by changing band tension
Useful for cardio circuits

description.en: The resistance band squat adds resistance to a standard bodyweight squat by standing on the band and holding the ends at your shoulders. It is essentially synonymous with the band squat — the band provides accommodating resistance, loading the top of the squat most heavily.

en: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold both ends of the band at your shoulders. Loop over shoulders for extra stability if the band is long enough.
Stand tall. Brace your core.
Sit your hips back and down into a squat.
Lower until your thighs are at or below parallel.
Drive through your full foot to stand against the band tension.
Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Repeat for the desired reps. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Adds progressive resistance to bodyweight squats
Accommodating resistance loads the top of the squat
Highly portable
Easy to scale
Useful when no weights are available
Mimics accommodating resistance in powerlifting

description.en: The ring high row is a variation of the ring inverted row where the pulling path is up to the face or chin instead of the chest. The higher pull point shifts emphasis to the upper back, rear delts, and rhomboids. It is a strong choice for posture and shoulder health.

en: Hang gymnastic rings at about waist height.
Grip the rings and lower yourself underneath.
Walk your feet forward until you are leaning back at an angle.
Position your body in a straight line.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Pull your body up to the rings, leading with the elbows out wide and high.
Bring the rings to face or chin level with elbows flared.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together hard at the top, then lower with control.
Targets upper back and rear delts
Builds posture and shoulder health
Strong rhomboid engagement
No weights required
Different stimulus than standard ring row
Useful for upper back training

description.en: The Rocky pull up pulldown alternates between pulling the bar down to the chest in front and pulling it down behind the neck. The alternating pattern hits the lats from two different angles in one set, building full upper back development. The name references the boxer character Rocky Balboa.

en: Sit at a lat pulldown station with a wide bar attachment.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip.
Sit tall with thighs secured under the pads.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Pull the bar down to your upper chest in front.
Slowly extend your arms back overhead.
On the next rep, pull the bar down behind your neck.
Alternate front and behind-the-neck pulls each rep.
Hits lats from two different angles
Builds full upper back development
Time-efficient lat training
Develops shoulder mobility through both pull paths
Useful for breaking through lat plateaus
Strong rhomboid engagement on behind-neck pulls

description.en: The roll glutes sitting on floor is a self myofascial release drill for the glutes. Sitting on a foam roller and rolling the glute releases knots from sitting and heavy training.

en: Sit on the floor with a foam roller under one glute.
Cross the working leg ankle over the opposite knee.
Lean back onto the hands for support.
Brace the core and shift the weight onto the roller.
Roll the glute slowly back and forth over the roller.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Adjust angle to cover the full glute.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the glutes.
Improves hip mobility.
Reduces sitting tightness.
Useful for runners.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The single straight leg stretch is a Pilates mat exercise where you lie on your back with head lifted, alternating pulling one straight leg toward your face while the other extends long and low. It builds lower-ab strength while dynamically stretching the hamstrings.

en: Lie on your back. Curl your head and shoulders off the floor. Look toward your navel.
Extend both legs straight. Lift your right leg up toward the ceiling.
Hold your right ankle (or calf) with both hands. Keep the left leg extended long, hovering a few inches off the floor.
Pulse the right leg twice toward your face with gentle pulls.
Switch legs in a scissoring motion — left leg comes up, right leg goes down.
Pulse the left leg twice. Continue alternating.
Keep your lower back pressed into the floor throughout. If it lifts, raise the lower leg higher.
Perform 8 to 12 reps per side. Move with control, not speed.
Builds lower-ab strength and endurance
Dynamically stretches the hamstrings
Teaches core stability with moving legs
Foundational Pilates mat exercise
No equipment needed
Improves hip flexibility and control

description.en: The ski step is a cardio exercise that mimics the lateral motion of downhill skiing — hopping side to side with both feet together while letting your arms swing naturally. It builds lateral power, ankle stability, and cardiovascular conditioning while engaging the obliques.

en: Stand tall with feet together. Bend your knees slightly into an athletic stance.
Hold your arms bent at your sides like you are holding ski poles.
Hop laterally to the right, keeping both feet together. Land softly on the balls of your feet.
Immediately hop to the left.
Continue hopping side to side rhythmically.
Let your arms swing naturally for balance — they may swing opposite to your legs.
Cover 6 to 12 inches with each hop.
Perform for 30 to 60 seconds per set.
Builds lateral power and quickness
Develops ankle stability
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Engages the obliques and core
No equipment needed
Useful warm-up exercise

description.en: The stationary bike walk is a low-intensity cardio drill performed on a stationary bike. The lifter pedals at a slow easy walking pace to build base cardiovascular endurance. The low intensity makes it ideal for warm-ups, recovery days, and beginners.

en: Adjust the bike seat to the correct height.
Mount the bike with both feet on the pedals.
Set a low resistance level.
Start pedaling at a slow easy pace.
Keep the cadence steady and relaxed.
Maintain the easy pace for the working time.
Use the time for warm-up or recovery.
Slow down and stop when finished.
Low-impact cardio
Useful warm-up drill
Easy on the joints
Builds base cardio
Useful recovery move
Strong beginner cardio

description.en: The bodyweight step-up is a single-leg compound exercise where you step up onto a box or bench using one leg, then step back down. It builds the quads, glutes, and hamstrings unilaterally while training balance and coordination. Box height controls the difficulty — higher boxes increase glute demand. It works anywhere with no equipment beyond a sturdy surface.

en: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench, roughly knee-height.
Plant your right foot fully on top of the box. Make sure your entire foot is on the surface.
Stand tall with chest up and core braced.
Drive through your right foot — pressing through the entire foot, especially the heel — to lift your body up onto the box.
Stand fully tall on top of the box with both feet planted. Squeeze your right glute hard.
Step the left foot back down to the floor under control. Keep most of your weight on the right leg.
Once your left foot is back on the floor, follow with your right foot. That is one rep.
Complete all reps on the right side, then switch. Resist pushing off the back leg. Progress by adding dumbbells or a barbell.
Builds quads, glutes, and balance with no equipment
Easily scalable by changing box height
Trains coordination and ankle stability
Exposes and corrects left-right imbalances
Carries over to climbing, hiking, and athletic movements
Works anywhere — needs only a sturdy surface

description.en: The suspender wide grip inverted row on floor is a back exercise using a suspension trainer with the handles spread wide. The wide grip emphasizes the upper back, rhomboids, and rear deltoids.

en: Set the suspension trainer handles to about chest height.
Grip the handles with a wide pronated grip.
Walk your feet forward and lean back to create body angle.
Brace the core and keep the body straight from heels to head.
Hang from the handles with arms fully extended.
Pull your chest up between the handles by driving the elbows back wide.
Squeeze the upper back at the top of the row.
Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Wide grip targets the upper back and rear delts.
Easy to scale by changing body angle.
Builds horizontal pulling strength.
Strengthens the rhomboids and trapezius.
Joint friendly with no spinal compression.
Travel friendly with portable suspension trainer.

description.en: The tiger tail tricep roll is a self-myofascial release move for the triceps. The lifter holds the stick massager and rolls it along the back of the upper arm. It is a useful recovery and warm-up move for tight triceps after pressing or arm work.

en: Sit or stand and let one arm hang at your side.
Hold the tiger tail stick by the handles with the other hand.
Place the roller across the back of the upper arm near the elbow.
Press down with moderate pressure into the tricep.
Roll the stick up the tricep toward the shoulder.
Pause on any tender spots to release the tissue.
Roll back down toward the elbow and repeat.
Continue several passes. Switch arms and repeat.
Releases tight triceps
Useful warm-up move
Speeds recovery
Easy to do anywhere
Trains tissue quality
Strong upper body recovery move

description.en: Triangle Pose (Trikonasana) is a foundational standing yoga pose where you stand with feet wide apart and reach down with one hand toward the front foot while extending the other arm straight up. It stretches the hamstrings, hips, and side body while building leg strength and balance. It is one of the most recognizable yoga poses.

en: Stand with feet about three to four feet apart. Turn your right foot out 90 degrees and your left foot in slightly.
Extend both arms parallel to the floor at shoulder height.
Reach your right hand far over your right foot, then hinge at the right hip.
Lower your right hand down to your right shin, ankle, foot, or the floor outside your right foot.
Extend your left arm straight up toward the ceiling. Stack your shoulders.
Keep both legs straight. Press through the outside edge of your back foot.
Look up at your top hand or forward if your neck is tight.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths. Switch sides.
Stretches the hamstrings of the front leg
Opens the hips and side body
Builds leg strength and balance
Stretches the obliques and intercostals
Improves spinal flexibility
Foundational standing yoga pose
